## Assessing the Factory Wiring in Your VW Polo

Before cutting any wires or routing new cables, you need to understand what is actually available under the dashboard of your 2003 VW Polo. The factory head unit likely utilized a pre-amplified setup or relied on the door modules for signal processing. When you install a Sony aftermarket stereo, that original unit is removed, stripping away any existing rear speaker connections unless they were hard-wired directly to the main harness.

The single wire you found near the central locking mechanism is almost certainly a control signal (likely 12V or PWM) used by the car's body control module (BCM) to actuate the lock/unlock motors, not an audio signal. Audio signals are low-voltage AC waveforms, whereas central locking uses DC voltage. Connecting speaker wires to the central locking harness will result in either silence or a loud click when you lock the doors. Do not attempt to splice into that line; the impedance and power requirements are completely different.

## Running the Signal from the Front to the Rear

Since your current setup only has front speakers, you must physically route new speaker wire from the Sony head unit at the dashboard to the rear door locations. The most reliable path is along the existing loom that runs from the firewall down to the footwells and up into the doors. You will likely find a large black or grey loom (the main harness) running under the dash.

To keep wiring hidden, strip back a section of this main harness near the firewall or behind the kick panel. Identify the ground wire in that bundle; you can often use it as a return path if your new speakers are low-impedance and you are careful, but the ideal setup is to run two dedicated wires per channel (positive and negative) for each rear speaker.

If you decide to route cables under the front passenger seat, be aware of the pinch points where the seat slides on its rails. Use high-quality speaker wire (typically 16 AWG or thicker for short runs) that has a smooth outer jacket to prevent fraying against metal rails. Secure the wire with zip ties every 12 to 18 inches to prevent vibration, which can eventually break the internal strands.

## Connecting to the Sony Head Unit

Once the wires reach the dashboard, you will connect them to the Sony stereo. Unlike the older factory head units that might have had a specific rear speaker harness, modern aftermarket stereos expect speakers to be connected directly to the back of the unit via dedicated terminals.

Look at the rear of your Sony unit; you should see four large binding posts labeled "Front," "Rear," and sometimes "Subwoofer." The wiring convention is color-coded:
*   **Red** connects to the Positive (+) terminal.
*   **Black** or **Blue** connects to the Negative (-) terminal.

You will need a speaker wire connector block (often called a speaker tap or pigtail harness) if you want to connect multiple speakers to the same output, but for a simple two-speaker rear setup, direct connection is best. Plug one red and one black wire into the "Rear" section of the stereo.

It is crucial to match polarity. If the front speakers push air out when the signal goes positive, the rear speakers must do the same. If you reverse the wiring on one rear speaker, the sound from that side will be out of phase with the rest of the system, causing a hollow or "cancelled" bass response and poor stereo imaging.

## Powering the Rear Door Speakers

Since there is no existing amplifier in your Polo's original setup, the Sony unit must provide sufficient power to drive the new rear speakers directly. Standard car stereos typically output around 20W to 40W per channel at maximum volume. If you install passive speakers (which come with their own voice coils and magnets), they will work fine as long as the impedance matches. Most aftermarket speakers are 4 Ohms or 8 Ohms, which is safe for standard head units.

Avoid using "active" speakers unless your Sony unit has a built-in amplifier section in the back, which most compact dash units do not. Active speakers require their own power source (12V) and ground, adding significant complexity to the wiring job inside the doors. Stick with passive speakers for this retrofit.

Before purchasing, verify the speaker wire you need. Standard speaker wire comes in rolls or pre-cut lengths with red and black conductors twisted together, usually with a PVC jacket that is durable enough for under-dash use. Ensure the connectors at the ends are stripped cleanly to allow for a solid crimp or solder connection to the binding posts on the Sony unit.
